c.tagline: North America's walled old city, French to its cobblestones.

taxi.fareNote: City-regulated meter (Taxi Coop Québec, Taxi Laurier), with a flat fare from the airport. Uber operates in the city, but Lyft does not serve Quebec City.

emergency.note: 911 is the all-in-one emergency number for police, fire and ambulance; operators serve callers in both French and English.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: The walled clifftop heart of Old Quebec, crowned by the Château Frontenac and the Dufferin Terrace and ringed by ramparts, museums and the Citadelle; the UNESCO must-see core where first-timers stay.

The steep Lower Town below the cliff, North America's oldest commercial district — a warren of 17th-century stone houses, the Petit-Champlain shopping lane and Place-Royale; postcard-pretty and central.
A lively neighbourhood just outside the walls along Rue Saint-Jean, full of indie shops, bars, cafes and the historic Épicerie J.A. Moisan; bohemian and endlessly walkable.
An elegant district of grand avenues, the Plains of Abraham park, major museums and the Grande Allée restaurant-and-club strip; upscale, green and lively after dark.
The regenerated Lower-Town working-class quarter turned trendy hub of tech offices, craft breweries, chef-driven restaurants and street art; the city's hippest, most local-feeling area.
lodging: Hôtel Palace Royal Centre-Ville Québec par JARO

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink.

transit.hours: RTC buses run roughly 5:30 AM to 1:00 AM, with a handful of overnight lines on weekends.
transit.note: Quebec City has no metro or tram — the RTC bus network, including the high-frequency Métrobus lines, is the only public transit (a tramway line is under construction). Old Quebec itself is best explored on foot.
transit.pay: Pay by exact-change cash on board or with the reloadable OPUS card and RTC Nomade app; single fares, day passes and books of tickets are available.

food.name: Poutine
food.desc: Quebec's national comfort dish: hot fries, squeaky fresh cheese curds and rich brown gravy, invented in the province in the 1950s.

places.name: Chez Ashton
places.note: Quebec City institution since 1969; the local benchmark for classic curd-and-gravy poutine.

places.name: Le Chic Shack
places.note: Hand-smashed potato poutines beside Chateau Frontenac; the forestiere with wild mushroom ragout stands out.

places.name: La Buche
places.note: Rustic cabane-style dining room hugely popular for its over-the-top poutines.

food.name: Tourtiere
food.desc: Deep-dish spiced meat pie of pork, beef or game baked in buttery pastry; the centrepiece of every Quebecois holiday table.

places.name: Aux Anciens Canadiens
places.note: In the 1676 Maison Jacquet; the city's best-known address for heritage Quebecois cooking.

places.name: La Buche
places.note: Hearty tourtiere served in a fur-and-snowshoe cabin setting locals also frequent.

places.name: Buffet de l'Antiquaire
places.note: Forty-year-old diner in the antiques quarter serving old-school home-style tourtiere.

food.name: Pouding chomeur
food.desc: Depression-era 'unemployed man's pudding': plain cake batter baked under hot maple syrup and cream so it caramelises into sauce.

places.name: Aux Anciens Canadiens
places.note: Serves the classic maple version alongside its heritage menu.

places.name: La Buche
places.note: Generous maple-drenched pouding chomeur, a favourite dessert order here.

places.name: Le Cochon Dingue
places.note: Long-running local bistro chain; reliable dessert stop after Petit-Champlain wandering.

food.name: Tire d'erable sur la neige (maple taffy)
food.desc: Boiling maple syrup poured onto packed snow and rolled onto a stick; a late-winter sugar-shack ritual sold in town during Carnaval.

places.name: Cabane a sucre Chez Dany
places.note: Working sugar shack with sugaring-season taffy on snow and a full cabane meal.

places.name: Erabliere du Cap
places.note: Popular family sugar shack near the city for the full spring maple experience.

places.name: Carnaval de Quebec grounds
places.note: Taffy stands set up across the winter carnival site each January and February.

food.name: Cretons
food.desc: Coarse pork-and-onion spread seasoned with cinnamon and clove, spread thick on toast at nearly every Quebec breakfast.

places.name: Buffet de l'Antiquaire
places.note: Classic Quebecois breakfast counter where cretons come with the morning plate.

places.name: Le Cochon Dingue
places.note: Dependable all-day breakfast with cretons on the traditional dejeuner.

places.name: Marche du Vieux-Port
places.note: Charcuterie stalls sell house-made cretons and other Quebec pork products to take away.

food.name: Soupe aux pois and feves au lard
food.desc: Yellow split-pea soup with salt pork and maple-sweetened baked beans, the workhorse pairing of old French-Canadian home cooking.

places.name: Aux Anciens Canadiens
places.note: Both dishes appear on the heritage menu in their most traditional form.

places.name: Buffet de l'Antiquaire
places.note: Homestyle soup and beans in a decades-old neighbourhood diner.

places.name: La Buche
places.note: Cabane-style menu built around exactly this kind of old-Quebec comfort food.

food.name: Caribou
food.desc: Warming Quebec winter drink of red wine fortified with spirits, maple syrup and spices, drunk from a plastic cane at Carnaval.

places.name: Carnaval de Quebec kiosks
places.note: The traditional place to drink caribou, sold in the carnival's souvenir canes.

places.name: Le Sacrilege
places.note: Much-loved local bar with a leafy terrace; pours caribou through the cold months.

places.name: La Buche
places.note: Serves caribou year-round alongside its Quebecois comfort menu.

food.name: Cidre de glace (ice cider)
food.desc: Quebec-invented dessert cider pressed from apples frozen on the tree, intensely sweet and apple-bright; often poured with cheese.

places.name: Cidrerie Verger Bilodeau
places.note: Family orchard and cidery on the island with free tastings of ice cider and apple products.

places.name: Cassis Monna & Filles
places.note: Award-winning blackcurrant and cider producer with a terrace bistro overlooking the river.

places.name: Marche du Vieux-Port
places.note: Producer stalls sell ice cider and other Ile d'Orleans drinks in the city centre.

landmarks: Château Frontenac
The world's most photographed hotel, a turreted 1893 railway castle crowning Cap Diamant and defining the skyline of Old Québec.
Quartier Petit Champlain
North America's oldest commercial district, a fairy-tale warren of stone boutiques, murals and the famous Breakneck Stairs below the cliff.
Place Royale
The cobbled square where Champlain founded New France in 1608, anchored by the 1688 stone church of Notre-Dame-des-Victoires.
Terrasse Dufferin
A grand boardwalk beside the Château Frontenac offering sweeping St. Lawrence views, street performers and a thrilling winter toboggan run.
Citadelle de Québec
A star-shaped British fortress still garrisoned by the Royal 22e Régiment, guarding the heights with summer changing-of-the-guard ceremonies.
Fortifications of Québec and Porte Saint-Louis
The only intact city walls north of Mexico, 4.6 kilometres of ramparts and gates encircling the UNESCO-listed old town.
Basilique-Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Québec
The mother church of Catholic North America, founded in 1647, glowing with gilded baldachin, stained glass and a rare holy door.
Plains of Abraham
The rolling battlefield park where Wolfe defeated Montcalm in 1759, now the city's beloved green space for picnics, concerts and cross-country skiing.
Montmorency Falls
A thundering 83-metre cataract higher than Niagara just outside the city, spanned by a suspension bridge, cable car and zipline.
Île d'Orléans
A pastoral island in the St. Lawrence minutes from downtown, dotted with ancestral farmhouses, vineyards, cideries and strawberry stands.

train.note: VIA Rail trains use the historic Gare du Palais, running along the Quebec City-Montreal corridor (~3h to Montreal) with connections onward to Ottawa and Toronto. There is no direct international rail service; cross-border Amtrak trains depart from Montreal.

bus.note: Orléans Express coaches link Quebec City with Montreal, Trois-Rivières and the Saguenay from the Gare du Palais bus terminal; for cross-border coaches to the United States you transfer in Montreal.

intl.to: Lévis (Canada) - across the St Lawrence from the Old Port

ferry.note: The Société des traversiers du Québec runs the frequent Québec-Lévis ferry across the St Lawrence; seasonal cruises and St Lawrence sightseeing boats also operate. All are domestic routes.

half.name: Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré
half.blurb: A vast neo-Romanesque basilica and major pilgrimage shrine on the Beaupré coast (~30 min).

half.name: Wendake
half.blurb: The Huron-Wendat First Nation community with a longhouse museum, waterfall and Indigenous cuisine (~20 min).

full.name: Baie-Saint-Paul (Charlevoix)
full.blurb: An artists' town amid the rolling Charlevoix hills and dramatic river scenery (~1h30).

full.name: Canyon Sainte-Anne
full.blurb: A dramatic gorge with waterfalls and suspension bridges near Beaupré (~40 min).

full.name: Mont-Sainte-Anne
full.blurb: A major ski and mountain-biking resort with gondola rides and Laurentian views (~40 min).
